# Closing its own loops: what an AI system that runs itself shows about the human in every step

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that AI agents can draft code, but a person still has to merge it, deploy it and check that it works. This paper argues otherwise: merging, deploying and checking are loops, and loops can be closed by code: checks that can fail, a lane that merges what passes, a probe that proves the deploy live, and a revert when it is not.

We state the common belief as properties that can fail, and test each against the records of a system that merges, deploys and checks its own work. Where it still depends on outside sessions, the paper says so with the number.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 6 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

A common belief holds that AI agents can draft code but a person must still merge it, deploy it and check that it works. Ultrastable is built to close those loops itself: a server-side lane merges green changes, every deploy is proven live against its commit, and every loop names its closing probe. [2]

This matters now because the usual answer, a person must merge, deploy and check AI work, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. Every loop says how it closes. Belief: an automated process needs a person to notice when it is done. Test: every registered loop declares a closing probe and a server-side owner. [2]
2. Merging needs no person. Belief: a change waits for a person to merge it. Test: median hours from a pull request opening to its merge. [2]
3. Deploys are checked by the system. Belief: someone has to check that a deploy really worked. Test: share of uploaded deploys proven live against their own commit. [2]
4. No person in the path. Belief: automation still needs a hand on the wheel. Test: human touches counted by the latest criticality tick. [2]
5. The system starts its own work. Belief: an AI system only does what a person asks. Test: share of merged pull requests the system's own loops opened. [2]
6. The system ships its own deploys. Belief: shipping to production needs a person. Test: verified deploys the system originated and executed itself. [2]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [1]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [2]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. Every loop says how it closes: a loop with no server-side owner fails the build (SERVER-OWNS-LOOPS-1, `foundation/loopowner.py`); each loop row carries its trigger, closing probe and owner (CLOCKWORK-1, `instances/ultrastable/loop-registry.json`)
2. Merging needs no person: the server-side sweeper merges a green pull request (AUTO-SHIP-CLEAN-1, `seed/worker/src/sweeper.js`); the lane reconciles conflicts with main and retries (DRAIN-ALL-1, `seed/worker/src/lane.js`)
3. Deploys are checked by the system: every deploy is read back and compared with its commit before it counts (HANDOFF-1, `deploy/deploy-workers.mjs`)
4. No person in the path: human touches are counted in the denominator of the system's own score (CRITICALITY-1, `foundation/criticality.py`)
5. The system starts its own work: the executor takes items from the queue in driver order and opens its own pull requests (SELF-REFERENCE-1, `foundation/executor.py`)
6. The system ships its own deploys: the tick wakes the executor, whose merged change deploys from the merge commit (SELF-REFERENCE-1, `seed/worker/src/executor.js`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. Every loop says how it closes. Put in place: a loop with no server-side owner fails the build. Check it with one number, share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner, and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
2. Merging needs no person. Put in place: the server-side sweeper merges a green pull request. Check it with one number, median hours from a pull request opening to its merge, and set a limit for it (<= 1.0 is the limit we use).
3. Deploys are checked by the system. Put in place: every deploy is read back and compared with its commit before it counts. Check it with one number, share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit, and set a limit for it (>= 0.95 is the limit we use).
4. No person in the path. Put in place: human touches are counted in the denominator of the system's own score. Check it with one number, human touches counted by the latest criticality tick, and set a limit for it (<= 0 is the limit we use).
5. The system starts its own work. Put in place: the executor takes items from the queue in driver order and opens its own pull requests. Check it with one number, share of merged pull requests opened by the system itself, and set a limit for it (>= 0.5 is the limit we use).
6. The system ships its own deploys. Put in place: the tick wakes the executor, whose merged change deploys from the merge commit. Check it with one number, verified deploys the system originated and executed itself (latest criticality tick), and set a limit for it (>= 1 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 3 of 6 of these checks pass today. Share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner reads 1.0 (n = 113; source: instances/ultrastable/loop-registry.json (declared)). Median hours from a pull request opening to its merge reads 0.15 (n = 64; source: GitHub REST pulls?state=closed, last 100 closed pull requests, fetched 2026-11-21T09:30:00Z). Share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit reads 1.0 (n = 40; source: ops/deploys.jsonl (same window)). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.

## 4. Trade-offs and limits

- Scale. One organization: 100 closed pull requests (64 merged) over 0.75 days. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 80% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the subcritical regime with 0 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Own R&D question set, regenerated from this system's records, version 2026-11-21; its findings may change in later versions.
